items.titel: UK’s MI5 warns local defense firms of Russian sabotage risk
items.anriss: The alert urges industry to respond immediately and “reduce opportunities for hostile actors to identify your organisation or people as targets, conduct hostile reconnaissance, and attack people, sites or operations.”

absaetze.t: BELFAST — British defense companies and local suppliers of military aid to Ukraine are at risk of Russian sabotage and arson attacks by Moscow’s proxies, the MI5 intelligence agency has warned.

In a joint alert [PDF] with the UK Ministry of Defence today, the National Protective Security Authority, an arm of the domestic spy service, said that Russia has recently “increased attempts to conduct sabotage against European defence-related facilities.” Such efforts are mainly shaped “by the use of proxy actors employing low-sophistication sabotage methodologies, such as arson,” added the alert.

The warning comes amid an increasing series of sabotage incidents against European defense firms region-wide. Both Estonian authorities and German authorities have publicly accused Russian intelligence of being behind sabotage plots in recent months.

In MI5’s note today, the agency notes that such activity “is intended to undermine support for Ukraine and may sit alongside other hostile activity, including intimidation of individuals, espionage and information operations….If your organisation supports military procurement or supplies equipment to Ukraine’s armed forces, it could be a target.”

The alert urges industry to respond immediately and “reduce opportunities for hostile actors to identify your organisation or people as targets, conduct hostile reconnaissance, and attack people, sites or operations.” That includes cutting down on digital footprints by “reviewing publicly-available information and removing unnecessary detail about products, facilities, operations and staff roles.”

Similarly, processes to detect “hostile reconnaissance” should incorporate development of a “security-conscious workforce that will recognise and report suspicious activity,” alongside establishing “clear site perimeters” and installation of “visible protective security measures as appropriate to your site’s profile and risk.”

Should an attack occur, the alert puts forward advice for minimizing its impact, stressing the need to “Develop, test and rehearse procedures for responding to suspicious activity, suspicious items and attack methodologies such as arson.”
The latest messaging for industry follows on from the UK convening secretive meetings with CEOs from the defense and critical infrastructure industries to address “threats posed by Russia.”

items.titel: FireAnt Mini Uncrewed Ground Vehicles Deploy Drone Detection Sensors In U.S. Army Test
items.anriss: A FireAnt uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV) was used to deploy small sensors capable of detecting hostile drones on the ground during a recent U.S. Army test exercise. Using UGVs to quickly establish even localized sensor networks could give …

absaetze.t: A FireAnt uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV) was used to deploy small sensors capable of detecting hostile drones on the ground during a recent U.S. Army test exercise. Using UGVs to quickly establish even localized sensor networks could give Army units a valuable, if not increasingly critical, boost in situational awareness of potential threats in the air and on the ground.

The sensor-toting FireAnt was among the capabilities demonstrated during the U.S. Army-led Needs-Driven Acquisition for Near-Term Operations Accelerated Capability II (NANO ACE II) event in October. The service only recently shared details about NANO ACE II, which took place at the Multidomain Training Area (MDTA) in Tan-Tan, Morocco, in cooperation with that country’s armed forces. The larger NANO ACE effort falls under the broader umbrella of the Army’s Operation Jailbreak, which has been focused primarily on devising new networking capabilities to link disparate systems.

“NANO ACE tested prototype systems that combine autonomous platforms with different payloads, mission management software and robust communications,” according to an Army release. “This test aimed to evaluate semi-autonomous capability sets that extend C-UAS [counter-uncrewed aerial systems] coverage and addressed an emergent U.S. joint force requirement to field integrated, autonomous sensing and effector capabilities on an accelerated acquisition timeline.”

“To meet these objectives, industry developers evaluated their systems against strict operational criteria, testing whether the platforms could operate independently on unimproved terrain while surviving a contested electronic warfare environment,” the release added. “Hosting this evaluation at the Moroccan owned MDTA underscores a deep appreciation for the Kingdom of Morocco’s ongoing partnership. AMTEC [the U.S. Army’s Africa Multi-Domain Training and Experimentation Center] is intended to leverage the region’s open electromagnetic spectrum, uncongested airspace and contested terrain to help combined forces test emerging technologies and maintain a decisive advantage in a complex strategic environment.”

In addition to AMTEC, representatives from the Army’s Global Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate, the Army Test and Evaluation Command (ATEC), U.S. Army Central (ARCENT), U.S. Africa Command (AFRICOM), the Army’s Southern European Task Force-Africa (SETAF-AF), and an unnamed “tactical U.S. Army division” participated in the event in Morocco.

Produced by Swarmbotics AI, FireAnt is a small 4×4 UGV designed to be readily reconfigurable for a wide variety of missions, including electronic warfare, surveillance and reconnaissance, and even being used as a one-way-attack munition. FireAnts are also capable of being employed in semi-autonomous swarms.

Pictures accompanying the Army’s release about NANO ACE II show the FireAnt configured to carry six small ground sensors, three each on two sets of rails angled to either side. The sensors slide off the rails and come to rest on a trio of small legs.

How the sensors in question function is not immediately clear, but they have a spherical central body and a slender antenna mast that extends upward. Sensors of this size and configuration could detect drones in various ways, including passively picking up signals they emit or by registering their acoustic signature.

As an aside, another FireAnt was spotted at a separate Army test exercise recently conducted at Fort Hood in Texas with what looks to be another type of deployable sensor system called Maple Seeds. These are “low-power, lightweight, disposable RF [radiofrequency]” sensors that “can locate, differentiate, and track targets in deep fires areas in contested A2/AD [anti-access/area denial] environments,” according to manufacturer MaXentric Technologies.
A separate version of FireAnt with a fixed acoustic sensor array has also been developed for NANO ACE, but it is not clear if it has been demonstrated at one of the Army’s test exercises yet.

Depending on how they are networked together, ground sensors deployed via UGV, as well as UGVs with their own sensor packages, could provide multiple streams of data for operators to fuse together. This, in turn, would help build a higher-fidelity picture of potential drone threats. That data could then be used to cue other more capable sensors to further track and categorize those objects of interest, as well as effectors to engage them. Ukrainian forces have notably been employing broadly similar kinds of distributed, multi-layered sensor architectures to spot incoming drone attacks and manage resources to respond to them for years now.

Using UGVs in this role also opens new options for deploying ground sensors in forward areas while also reducing risks to human operators. A swarm of sensor-toting robotic vehicles would be able to seed that coverage across a broader area faster. Army testing earlier this year involving a Bradley Fighting Vehicle acting as a carrier for FireAnts demonstrated how UGVs could be brought to forward areas before pushing ahead of friendly forces, regardless of what their assigned tasks might be.

There’s a cost component to this equation, too. Whether seeded via UGV or other means, unattended ground sensors offer a lower-cost option for expanding coverage, especially in areas where it would be too risky to deploy more conventional radars and other assets. If they operate passively, the sensors themselves could be challenging for enemy forces to find and neutralize them once they’re in place.

While the recent NANO ACE event in Morocco was focused on counter-drone capabilities, sensors deployed in this way could be used to detect potential threats on the ground, as well. It’s understandable, though, that the Army is most interested currently in providing units new ways to spot incoming uncrewed attackers, a threat ecosystem that is only continuing to expand in scale and scope. Soldiers can expect drone attacks to come at the tactical edge, in rear areas, and everywhere in between in future conflicts.

Recent experiences from the war with Iran, as well as other conflicts in the Middle East and ongoing fighting in Ukraine, have shown that various tiers of uncrewed attackers can easily be layered in with other weapons and approach targets from multiple vectors simultaneously. In Ukraine, a tactic has also emerged where human operators fly small first-person-view kamikaze drones to forward areas where they then lie in wait on the ground like remotely-operated land mines. All of this only increases challenges for defenders when it comes to just spotting threats, let alone prioritizing and engaging them.

It should also be stressed here that unattended ground sensors are in no way new to the U.S. military. Historically, fixed-wing aircraft, helicopters, and small teams on the ground have been used to emplace them. The best-known example of this is Operation Igloo White, the then-state-of-the-art Vietnam War effort to remotely monitor movement along the Ho Chi Minh Trail. Igloo White also proved to be controversial due to its cost, complexity, and mixed results.

The Army and other branches of the U.S. military have also previously experimented with using uncrewed aerial systems to deploy sensors on the ground in forward areas, as well as act as readily relocatable sensor nodes themselves. The service has raised the possibility of using high-altitude balloons for this purpose, as well.

There are still potential hurdles for the Army to clear before it can employ UGV-deployed ground sensors on a broader scale. As noted, NANO ACE is an offshoot of Operation Jailbreak, and networking all of these nodes together could present challenges. Army officials have also talked in the past about how expanding distributed sensor coverage can produce data overload.

“One of the big problems we identified in this particular scenario is going to be we have too much data, and we haven’t been able to correlate it in the way that we want to provide it to the warfighter,” now-retired Lt. Gen. Scott McKean, then Project Convergence experiment director and deputy commander of Army Futures Command, said following a test exercise back in 2022. “A few years ago, we wouldn’t have had that problem because we weren’t even talking to each other, and our machines certainly wouldn’t be talking to each other. And so that’s a huge step forward, the fact that we are all sharing data. … We have the capability right now to take multiple communication pathways. Some of those are very military-specific. Some of those are actually quite commercial. And we can use those in multiple ways, so if one is denied, we switch to another one.”

“We still need to keep working on how we standardize the data so that we’re all able to access it and we’re all able to share it across services and platforms,” then-Secretary of the Army Christine Wormuth also said at the time. “I think we’re making progress on that, but there’s still work that has to be done. … We’re now able to tap into a huge volume of data. A lot of the challenge is going to be figuring out how we process that as quickly as we can, and I think we did see some real improvements in terms of how quickly we were able to take information and change it into what I would call more actionable knowledge. The other thing I think we have to do is commanders are going to have to figure out what are the critical information requirements that they need.”
These are areas where developments in artificial intelligence and machine learning could help human operators sift through the data.

The Army has also struggled with attempts to field larger uncrewed platforms in recent years. This stands in the face of global trends, especially in Ukraine, where smaller UGVs have steadily become a fixture in the ongoing conflict.

FireAnt increasingly looks to be at the forefront of Army efforts to integrate UGVs of various types into its broader force structure. The recent NANO ACE II event has highlighted another potentially important role for these uncrewed platforms as a way to help commanders get a better sense of the battlespace around them in the air and on the ground.

items.titel: Frida Kahlo-inspired health initiative and Ukrainian veterans exhibition among winners of prize celebrating innovative cultural projects
items.anriss: Five non-profit cultural organisations from across Europe have won the 2026 Art Explora awards, enjoying a share of €180,000 in total prize funds

absaetze.t: The charity Art Explora has revealed the five winners of the 2026 edition of its Académie des beaux-arts European Award, which recognises innovative work by non-profit arts and culture organisations in Europe. They are Polish performing arts foundation Jazdaa Polska!, Spanish art and health organisation Cultura en Vena, the French library charity Bibliothèques Sans Frontières, UK literary organisation London Writers Centre and Slovakian theatre company RAMAGU. The organisations were awarded funds ranging from €30,000-50,000, shared from a total £180,000.

The winners were announced at an award ceremony at the Victoria and Albert Museum in London on the evening of 24 November. Each of them, apart from RAMAGU—which won an audience choice award—was selected by an international jury, which included several members of the Académie des beaux-arts in Paris, such as the illustrator Emmanuel Guibert and the sculptor Eva Jospin; Vanja Kaludjercic, the director of the International Film Festival Rotterdam; and Antonija Letinić, a cultural development consultant in Croatia. Frédéric Jousset, the French entrepreneur and founder of Art Explora, was also a juror.

Cultura en Vena, who has been awarded €40,000, will puts the funds towards its Arte Ambulatorio project, which brings reproductions of works of art and other forms of creative programming into hospital spaces. The new phase of the project will involve an exhibition inspired by the work of Frida Kahlo, as well as live music sessions and creative writing workshops for children. Previous Arte Ambulatorio interventions focused on the work of the Spanish artists Francisco Goya and Joaquín Sorolla.

According to the organisation, “Frida Kahlo’s artistic universe offers a powerful entry point into themes closely connected to the hospital experience: the body, pain, vulnerability, identity, resilience, emotional expression and care.”

“Cultura en Vena takes art as seriously as care,” Jousset tells The Art Newspaper. He says the jury was convinced by “their rigour”. “They measure their impact and keep improving each exhibition based on patients’ and staff feedback,” he continues. “With over 23,000 peopkeople reached last year, they are one of the leading voices in arts and wellbeing in Spain.”

Bibliothèques Sans Frontières, meanwhile, will put its €50,000 award towards its L’autre retour project. The initiative involves workshops within which Ukrainian veterans are invited to draw, read and write with members of their community outside of a clinical environment, in an effort to help with reintegration after the military. The charity then plans to tour some of the works in Ukraine, as well as show them at the European Commission in Brussels.
“This project shows art as an act of rebuilding,” Jousset says.

The additional funded projects include developing touch-based choreography with blind and partially-sighted people in Poland (Jazdaa Polska!), making Lewisham in London the UK’s first “Borough of Literature” (London Writers Centre), and creating documentary theatre with minority groups in rural Slovakia (RAMAGU).

items.titel: Streit um Schweizer Auftritt von Opern-Star Anna Netrebko

absaetze.t: Russische Opernsängerin tritt am 30. November in Basel auf Streit um Schweizer Auftritt von Anna Netrebko
Streit um Schweizer Auftritt von Anna Netrebko
Anna Netrebkos Basel-Debüt sorgt für Protest: Rund 750 Menschen haben eine Petition gegen das Konzert vom 30. November unterzeichnet. Der Veranstalter will die Sopranistin dennoch auftreten lassen.
Publiziert: 24.11.2026 um 16:12 Uhr
Aktualisiert: 24.11.2026 um 16:14 Uhr
Anna Netrebko tritt am 30. November erstmals in Basel auf, trotz Kritik an ihrer Nähe zu Putin
Eine Petition des Ukrainischen Vereins Schweiz fordert die Absage und zählt rund 750 Unterschriften
Veranstalter Thomas Dürr hält am Konzert fest, die ukrainische Community plant einen Protest

Die einen feiern sie als eine der grössten Operndiven unserer Zeit, andere boykottieren sie und werfen ihr Nähe zum russischen Präsidenten Wladimir Putin (74) vor. Am 30. November tritt die Sopranistin Anna Netrebko (55) erstmals in Basel auf – doch ihr Gastspiel im Stadtcasino löst heftigen Widerstand aus. Eine Onlinepetition fordert die Absage des Konzerts.

«Basel darf nicht zur Bühne für die Rehabilitierung von Symbolfiguren des Putin-Regimes werden», schreiben die Ersteller der Petition vom Ukrainischen Verein Schweiz, Ortsgruppe Basel. «Wenn renommierte Bühnen Personen eine Plattform bieten, deren öffentliche Biografie mit der Unterstützung eines Kriegsverbrecher-Regimes verbunden ist, wird dies unweigerlich als Form symbolischer Legitimation wahrgenommen.» Rund 750 Menschen haben die Petition bislang unterzeichnet.
Diverse Opern boykottieren Netrebko

Es wäre nicht die erste Absage wegen ihrer Putin-Nähe. Die New Yorker Metropolitan Opera und die Bayerische Staatsoper warfen Netrebko aus dem Programm, weil sie sich nach Start des russischen Angriffskriegs auf die Ukraine in ihren Augen nicht genügend von Putin distanzierte. 2024 platzte zudem ein geplanter Auftritt im KKL Luzern. Auch das Opernhaus Zürich strich die Russin zunächst aus dem Programm, holte sie im November 2025 aber für «La Forza del Destino» wieder auf die Bühne (Blick berichtete). Im Juli 2027 ist Netrebko zudem als Mimì in der Oper «La Bohème» im Zürcher Opernhaus zu sehen.

Im März 2022 nahm Netrebko Stellung: «Ich verurteile den Krieg gegen die Ukraine ausdrücklich und meine Gedanken sind bei den Opfern dieses Krieges und ihren Familien», schrieb sie damals. «Ich bin weder Mitglied einer politischen Partei noch bin ich mit irgendeinem Führer Russlands verbunden. Ich erkenne und bedauere, dass meine Handlungen oder Aussagen in der Vergangenheit zum Teil falsch interpretiert werden konnten.» Sie habe Putin in ihrem Leben nur eine Handvoll Male getroffen, «vor allem im Rahmen von Verleihungen von Auszeichnungen für meine Kunst oder bei der Eröffnungsfeier der Olympischen Spiele».
Vorbereitungen laufen normal

Konzertveranstalter Thomas Dürr lässt sich davon nicht beirren. Die Vorbereitungen laufen «normal», sagt er auf Anfrage von Blick. «Ich kann die Kritik nicht nachvollziehen. Besonders die Frage, ob sich Anna Netrebko genügend distanziert hat, befremdet mich, müssen wir jetzt alle eine Einheitsmeinung haben?» Seit fünf Jahren stehe er mit Anna Netrebko in Kontakt, um sie nach Basel zu holen. Von Veranstaltungsverboten halte er nichts. «Das bringt sicher keinen Frieden», so Dürr weiter.

Schon im Mai 2024 wollte Dürr ans Netrebko-Konzert in Luzern – zusammen mit seiner Partnerin Irina Beller (54), die selbst russische und ukrainische Wurzeln hat. «Das wurde auf Kosten der Luzerner Steuerzahler abgesagt. Für mich unverständlich», sagt Dürr.
Neben der Petition droht auch auf der Strasse Gegenwind: Laut «Basler Zeitung» plant die ukrainische Community am Konzertabend eine Protestaktion direkt vor dem gegenüberliegenden Puppenmuseum.

items.titel: Le hip-hop en quête d'une reconnaissance mondiale à l'Unesco
items.anriss: Contre-culture devenue mouvement mondial majeur, le hip-hop, incarné notamment par des stars du rap, met un pied à l'Unesco. Une charte ouvrant la perspective d'une inscription au patrimoine culturel immatériel de l'humanité a été signée …

absaetze.t: Contre-culture devenue mouvement mondial majeur, le hip-hop, incarné notamment par des stars du rap, met un pied à l'Unesco. Une charte ouvrant la perspective d'une inscription au patrimoine culturel immatériel de l'humanité a été signée cette semaine.

Cette première étape, à Paris, est impulsée par les délégations de la République du Congo et de la République démocratique du Congo, deux pays ayant œuvré à l'inscription de la rumba congolaise sur cette liste en 2021.

"Les trajectoires (des deux musiques, ndlr) ont été comparées de façon à ce que nous puissions porter l'inscription officielle du hip-hop au patrimoine mondial", explique Dreyfus Louyebo, président du comité de liaison avec l'Unesco.

"Le hip-hop est une culture internationale: même s'il est né aux Etats-Unis, il vient d'un certain nombre de genres musicaux qui étaient sur le continent africain", dont la rumba congolaise, ajoute-t-il.
Dans la continuité des griots

Apparu dans les années 1970, dans les block parties du Bronx, ce mouvement culturel se décline à travers le DJing, le graffiti, la breakdance, la mode et le rap, lui-même abreuvé par le funk et la soul notamment.

"La musique hip-hop est une continuité de ce que faisaient les griots de l'Afrique de l'Ouest" car le rap s'inscrit dans la lignée de ces "conteurs qui transmettent l'histoire, la généalogie, la critique sociale, en rythme", abonde Alexandre Kirchhoff, patron du label Capitol (Universal), chargé de rassembler les professionnels de l'industrie musicale autour du projet.

Après les Etats-Unis, terre du label new-yorkais Def Jam Recordings et des superstars Jay-Z, Kendrick Lamar et Snoop Dogg, "la France est la deuxième nation du hip-hop au monde", estiment les défenseurs de cette reconnaissance par l'Organisation des Nations unies pour l'éducation, la science et la culture.
Un "métissage énorme"
En haut des classements, le rap compte d'ailleurs dans son vivier de nombreux artistes d'origine congolaise dont Gims, Ninho, Shay, SDM, Youssoupha et Tiakola.

"Vous vous rendez compte des chiffres que les petits frères font? Il faut reconnaitre la force de cette culture", souligne Passi, artiste franco-congolais parmi les pionniers du rap français, à l'époque de Suprême NTM, IAM et MC Solaar. Engagé, dansant ou poétique, "c'est un genre qui se renouvelle, qui vit avec son temps", loue-t-il.

"Il y a un métissage énorme. Dans le hip-hop, on peut tout mélanger. Tout ça fait un beau feu d'artifice!", s'enthousiasme Sidney, figure du mouvement en France avec l'émission de télévision H.I.P. H.O.P., qui vient de publier 'Hip-hop - Des origines à nos jours'.

Après la charte, un comité intergouvernemental doit être instauré pour bâtir cette candidature multinationale. Les Etats-Unis ont été associés à la démarche, mais plus pour longtemps: ils se retirent officiellement de l'Unesco le 31 décembre, sur décision de Donald Trump.

items.titel: Londres a enfin son Carnavalet : le London Museum dévoile 450 000 ans d’histoire dans un ancien marché de la City
items.anriss: King’s Cross St. Pancras, terminus ! Tout le monde descend de l’Eurostar. À une station de métro, sur les lignes Circle, Hammersmith & City ou Metropolitan, se trouve le nouveau London Museum, l’un des plus grands musées au monde dédiés à …

absaetze.t: Le London Museum est à Londres ce que le musée Carnavalet est à Paris : un hommage à une ville et à ses habitants, le témoin d’une histoire urbaine plurimillénaire. Et il rouvre ses portes dans un ancien marché couvert au cœur de la City. Visite guidée avec la directrice Sharon Ament, qui prêche solidarité et joie de vivre.

King’s Cross St. Pancras, terminus ! Tout le monde descend de l’Eurostar. À une station de métro, sur les lignes Circle, Hammersmith & City ou Metropolitan, se trouve le nouveau London Museum, l’un des plus grands musées au monde dédiés à une ville. Fusionné en 1965 avec le Guildhall Museum de 1826, sous le nom de Museum of London, il recouvre donc son nom d’origine. Pourquoi ? « Moins de syllabes à prononcer. Et clin d’œil au British Museum ! », plaisante sa directrice, Sharon Ament, partisane de la joie de vivre dans un monde de plus en plus fractionné. Autrefois située près du London Wall, au nord de la City, l’institution a déménagé dans le General Market de Smithfield, ancien marché couvert dont la rénovation, entamée il y a dix ans sous l’égide des architectes Stanton Williams et Asif Khan, touche à sa fin.
Un parcours en trois temps et Banksy en point de mire

Le nouveau London Museum s’articule autour de trois espaces. Chacun incarne une temporalité précise. La West Poultry Avenue, couverte et fermée à ses extrémités, accueille désormais les visiteurs sous le nom de « Real Time » (Temps réel). Aux murs, des écrans diffusent des informations en temps réel sur Londres et ses habitants et, à heures fixes, un joyeux ballet de pigeons. « Toute la fantaisie du musée ressort ici. L’allégresse est essentielle. Nos collections ne racontent pas que des histoires heureuses… » Au centre de ce hall lumineux et animé trône Piranhas, guérite de police transformée par Banksy en aquarium.
Le « General Market » du London Museum depuis le hall d’entrée principal situé sur West Poultry Avenue. ©Hufton+Crow
Un rez-de-chaussée convivial au cœur de la vie londonienne

À gauche se profile le Poultry Market, encore en activité, qui abritera dès 2028 deux espaces d’exposition, un centre pédagogique et des réserves. À droite, l’entrée de l’ancien General Market de Smithfield mène dans la section « Our Time » (Notre temps), carrefour de détente et de rencontre, ponctué de treize grandes installations incarnant le quotidien des Londoniens. Certaines ont été réalisées spécialement pour le lieu, comme cette girafe aux oreilles mécaniques modelée sur Molly, résidente du ZSL London Zoo qui faisait la une des journaux britanniques durant la crise sanitaire. À côté du restaurant se dresse un standard téléphonique privé (PBX), qui servait à établir les communications internes et externes au sein de Buckingham Palace. Du thé et des biscuits seront servis gratuitement au Syd’s Coffee, food truck offert au musée par la petite-fille de son fondateur.

« Our Time » dans le Linbury Hall est un lieu de rencontre animé au cœur du London Museum, aménagé dans l’ancienne salle des marchés du General Market. Tout autour, un restaurant, une boutique et un espace d’exposition destiné aux familles et aux écoles côtoient 13 grandes installations phares qui explorent les différentes façons dont les Londoniens se sont rassemblés au fil du temps. ©Hufton+Crow
Au sous-sol, les collections enrichies racontent un demi-million d’années d’histoire

Au niveau inférieur, plongée dans « Past Time » (Temps passé), aménagé dans les voûtes souterraines découvertes au cours des travaux de restauration. Cette section abrite 5 000 pièces (sur un total de 7 millions environ), qui retracent 450 000 ans d’histoire. Parmi les nouveautés, la Bloomberg Collection rassemble plus de 14 000 artefacts romains, dont des tablettes d’écriture exhumées lors de fouilles archéologiques. Quant à la Goldsmiths’Gallery, elle révèle la Cheapside Hoard, un ensemble de bijoux des périodes élisabéthaine et jacobéenne. Mention spéciale pour la scénographie, qui repose sur un subtil dosage entre outils multimédias et objets tangibles.
« Past Time » est l’exposition permanente gratuite du musée, où les visiteurs découvriront les personnages et les événements qui ont façonné Londres tout au long de son histoire. ©Hufton+Crow
Printemps 2027 sur des rails : les premières expositions temporaires

Clou du spectacle : une large fenêtre donne sur la voie ferrée qui longe le sous-sol. Autrefois utilisée par la Great Northern Railway pour acheminer les marchandises vers le marché de Smithfield, la voilà empruntée aujourd’hui par le réseau Thameslink. Des assises invitent les visiteurs à s’arrêter pour regarder les rames défiler sous leurs yeux. Il faudra attendre le printemps 2027 pour découvrir les expositions temporaires qui se succéderont dans un autre espace souterrain de 800 m².
